facts.statement: Elasmosaurus lived in North America approximately 80.6 to 77 million years ago.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus () is a genus of plesiosaur that lived in North America during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period, at about 80.6 to 77 million years ago.

facts.statement: The first Elasmosaurus specimen was discovered in 1867 near Fort Wallace, Kansas, and named E. platyurus by Edward Drinker Cope in 1868.
facts.quote: The first specimen was discovered in 1867 near Fort Wallace, Kansas, US, and was sent to the American paleontologist Edward Drinker Cope, who named it E.platyurus in 1868.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Elasmosaurus was found in a ravine within the Pierre Shale formation.
facts.quote: Turner discovered the bones of a large fossil reptile in a ravine in the Pierre Shale formation

facts.statement: The neck of Elasmosaurus was approximately 7.1 meters long.
facts.quote: The neck alone was around 7.1 m long.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus had 72 neck vertebrae, the second highest number known for any animal, with Albertonectes having at least three more.
facts.quote: Along with its relative Albertonectes, it was one of the longest-necked animals to have lived, with the second largest number of neck vertebrae known, 72, at least 3 fewer than Albertonectes.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurids likely fed on small fish and marine invertebrates, possibly using gastroliths to aid digestion.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurids probably ate small fish and marine invertebrates, seizing them with their long teeth, and may have used gastroliths (stomach stones) to help digest their food.

facts.statement: Elasmosaurus fossils are found in the Pierre Shale formation, representing marine deposits from the Western Interior Seaway.
facts.quote: Elasmosaurus is known from the Pierre Shale formation, which represents marine deposits from the Western Interior Seaway.

facts.statement: It is debated whether a fragmentary specimen from Germany belongs to the genus Elasmosaurus.
facts.quote: A fragmentary specimen from Germany may belong to this genus.

facts.statement: The circumstances surrounding Theophilus Hunt Turner's discovery of the type specimen remained unknown until his letters were published in 1987.
facts.quote: The circumstances around Turner's discovery of the type specimen were not covered in Cope's report, and remained unknown until Turner's letters were published in 1987.

facts.statement: Cope initially reconstructed Elasmosaurus with the skull at the end of the tail, a mistake later identified by Joseph Leidy.
facts.quote: Cope had apparently concluded that the tail vertebrae belonged to the neck, since the jaws had been found at that end of the skeleton, even though the opposite end terminated in the axis and atlas bones that are found in the neck.

facts.statement: Joseph Leidy concluded that Elasmosaurus was identical to Discosaurus, a genus he had named in 1851.
facts.quote: Leidy also concluded that Elasmosaurus was identical to Discosaurus, a plesiosaur he had named in 1851.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope initially believed the original Elasmosaurus material consisted of two different animals, referring to a smaller part as Discosaurus carinatus in a 1868 letter.
facts.quote: Cope initially thought it consisted of two specimens of different animals – in an 1868 letter to LeConte, Cope had referred to the supposed "smaller specimen" as Discosaurus carinatus.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Elasmosaurus was redescribed in detail in 2005 by the German paleontologist Sven Sachs.
facts.quote: It was only redescribed in detail in 2005 by the German paleontologist Sven Sachs.

facts.statement: The only definite specimen of Elasmosaurus is the incomplete holotype cataloged as ANSP 10081.
facts.quote: Today, the incomplete holotype specimen, cataloged as ANSP 10081, is the only definite specimen of Elasmosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2013, Sven Sachs rediscovered a lost neck vertebra in storage, revising the count of cervical vertebrae in the holotype from 71 to 72.
facts.quote: In 2013 an incomplete neck vertebra centrum of the holotype that had been mentioned by Cope but thought to have been lost was rediscovered in storage by Sachs, and the neck vertebra count was revised from 71 to 72.

facts.statement: Fossils potentially belonging to the holotype were found by Benjamin Franklin Mudge in 1871 but are likely lost.

facts.statement: In 2007, Leslie Noè and Marcela Gómez-Pérez doubted that additional fossil elements found near the original locality belonged to the type specimen or to Elasmosaurus.

facts.statement: Jane P. Davidson and Michael J. Everhart concluded that the missing pectoral and pelvic girdle fossils were most likely destroyed in Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins' workshop.
